questions.q: What is the formula of the tracking signal?
options: Running sum of errors / running MAD
why: Correct.
That is a relative error (like WAPE), not the tracking signal.
This measures spread, not accumulated bias.
A single point cannot show a slow bias.

questions.q: Errors (actual − forecast) over 5 days: +4, +6, +2, +8, +5. What is the TS at day 5?
questions.why: RSFE = 25. MAD = (4+6+2+8+5)/5 = 5. TS = 25 / 5 = 5, above the limit 4.

questions.q: Two forecasts have the same MAD. Forecast A has errors that alternate +5 and −5. Forecast B has errors that are always +5. Which has a large tracking signal?
why: A's errors cancel, so RSFE stays near 0.
Correct: B's errors add up, so TS grows.
Only B is biased.
B grows past any limit.

questions.q: Which are good practices for forecast alerts? (pick all)
options: Link each alert to a runbook
why: It removes hard-day effects.
It avoids reacting to one day.
One global number hides bad segments.
People need to know what to do.

questions.q: Scenario: item sales are often 0 or 1. Your dashboard shows MAPE = 'infinite' for many items. What do you switch to?
options: WAPE (sum of absolute errors / sum of actuals), at group level
why: You would hide the hard items.
Correct: the denominator is a total, so zeros do not break it.
Log does not fix zeros.
Accuracy is a classification metric.

questions.q: Scenario: TS jumps to 9 on day 2 of a new model. Should you alarm?
options: No, use a minimum number of periods first; TS is unstable with few points
why: Early values are huge because MAD is based on two points.
Correct.
An absolute MAE rule is not the point here.
Retraining on two days of data is risky.
